choiceReview.text: PERT is dosed in lipase units and taken with every relevant meal, snack, formula, or feed.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: PERT is dosed by protease units, regardless of the stated lipase strength.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: One morning oral dose provides enzyme coverage for every later meal.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: All pancreatic enzyme products can be exchanged by capsule count.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Lipase units determine PERT dosing. Replacement accompanies relevant intake; continuous feeds need an explicit product and CF-team plan. Protease units, a once-daily oral schedule, and capsule-count substitution do not establish equivalent exposure.

choiceReview.text: Give at the start of intake, distribute during prolonged meals when directed, and titrate within safe limits to symptoms and growth.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Take the entire daily dose before breakfast, including doses intended for later snacks.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Take meal doses only when steatorrhea appears after eating.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Crush the delayed-release particles into food to improve release.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Oral enzymes accompany eating. The CF team may distribute a prolonged-meal dose. Delayed dosing, consolidating separate meal doses, or destroying the coating interferes with appropriate delivery.

choiceReview.text: Review lipase units per capsule, weight, meal and snack pattern, fat, timing, swallowing, storage, stool, pain, growth, and adherence.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review capsule count alone because every capsule has the same lipase content.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review the meal dose but omit snacks from the daily total.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review stool symptoms alone and assume normal stools prove adequate absorption.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Connect strength and intake to weight and total daily exposure, then examine delivery, storage, symptoms, growth, and adherence. Capsule count alone and symptom-only titration omit important dose and outcome information.

choiceReview.text: Prescribing capsules without calculating total lipase exposure can hide severe underdosing or unsafe escalation.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Recording lipase units per capsule and the number of capsules taken
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Checking each meal dose against the patient weight
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Adding meal and snack exposures to review the daily lipase total
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: The book bases pancreatic-enzyme doses on the lipase component, not capsule count alone. Product strength, units per intake and the daily total must be connected to weight and the prescribed schedule to identify underdosing or unsafe escalation.

choiceReview.text: For Creon after 12 months of age, doses above 2,500 lipase units/kg/meal, 10,000 units/kg/day, or 4,000 units/g fat ingested/day require further investigation.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: A meal dose below 2,500 units/kg makes the daily total irrelevant.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: A daily dose below 10,000 units/kg makes the meal dose irrelevant.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: The 4,000-unit fat boundary refers to grams of protein eaten.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Check all applicable boundaries. A satisfactory meal value does not authorize an excessive daily or fat-based exposure. The fat-based measure uses ingested fat, not protein; doses beyond guidance require investigation and documented justification.

choiceReview.text: Audit timing, adherence, storage, diet, acid, constipation, infection, and alternate disease before escalating beyond boundaries.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Increase PERT automatically for every abdominal complaint.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Increase PERT until stools look normal without reviewing total exposure.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Add a proton pump inhibitor to every capsule regimen before reviewing timing or adherence.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Poor response can reflect delivery, diet, motility, hyperacidity, liver disease, or another gastrointestinal diagnosis. Review these factors before escalating; neither abdominal symptoms nor stool appearance alone establishes a need for more enzyme, and acid suppression is not universal.

choiceReview.text: Review weight, lipase per capsule, capsules per intake, meals, snacks, total daily units, symptoms, stool, growth, pain, and colon history.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review only the capsule count and omit lipase strength and body weight
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review one meal dose but omit snacks and the daily total
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review nutritional intake but omit abdominal symptoms and the colonic-risk history
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: The book connects lipase-unit dose limits with rare fibrosing colonopathy and colonic strictures and monitors abdominal symptoms, intake, weight, height and stools. Capsule strength, intake count and body weight allow the meal and daily exposures to be checked; the colon history is a practical review of the stated safety risk.

choiceReview.text: Escalating very high PERT for every abdominal symptom can increase fibrosing-colonopathy risk without treating the true cause.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Checking lipase units per meal and total daily exposure before a dose change
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Reviewing stool, intake, growth and abdominal symptoms together
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Recognizing abdominal pain as a possible treatment adverse effect
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: The book lists abdominal pain as an adverse effect and associates very high lipase exposure with fibrosing colonopathy and colonic strictures. More enzyme is therefore not a safe automatic response to every abdominal symptom. Review dose and the clinical findings before escalation.

choiceReview.text: Nutrition plans address energy, protein, fat, salt, vitamins A, D, E, and K, body composition, and changing metabolic risk.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Nutrition in CF always requires unlimited calories irrespective of weight or modulator response.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: A normal weight excludes fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and ends monitoring.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: An effective modulator makes PERT and vitamin replacement unnecessary without reassessment.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Nutrition care integrates intake, absorption, vitamin status, and current phenotype. Weight or modulator response alone does not establish adequate micronutrients or restored pancreatic function.

choiceReview.text: Individualize intake and replacement from phenotype, labs, growth or weight trajectory, malabsorption, modulator response, and goals.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Keep the original high-calorie plan indefinitely despite major weight and blood-pressure changes.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Stop PERT whenever weight rises after modulator therapy.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Treat nutritional decline by calories alone without reviewing malabsorption or food access.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Reassess current needs and outcomes. Modulators can alter weight and absorption, but changing PERT needs pancreatic evaluation; a historical calorie prescription or calorie-only response may miss the limiting mechanism.

choiceReview.text: Review intake, access, stool, PERT, weight history, growth, strength, body composition, vitamin levels, sodium, glucose, liver, and bone.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review current weight alone and omit the trajectory, vitamins, and stool pattern.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review the enzyme prescription but omit actual use and access to food.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review calorie intake but omit glucose, liver, and bone complications.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: A multidomain assessment connects nutrition with digestion and systemic disease. A weight-only, prescription-only, or calorie-only review leaves important causes and consequences unexamined.

choiceReview.text: Preserving a universal unlimited-calorie message after major modulator-associated weight gain can ignore cardiometabolic health.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Reassessing dietary quality when the weight trajectory changes
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Checking blood pressure and current salt needs after modulator response
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Continuing appropriate vitamin and pancreatic-function assessment
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: An unlimited-calorie message can become inappropriate as phenotype changes. Reviewing quality, salt needs, and vitamin or pancreatic status is appropriate; modulator-associated weight gain does not justify abandoning nutritional surveillance.

choiceReview.text: Annual two-hour OGTT begins by age 10, using 1.75 g/kg glucose up to 75 g; A1c alone is insufficient, and established CFRD is treated with insulin.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: A1c alone is the preferred annual screen when CF is clinically stable.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Annual CFRD screening begins only after weight loss or polyuria appears.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Oral glucose-lowering drugs routinely replace insulin as first-line CFRD treatment.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: OGTT is the recommended annual screen by age 10, with the pediatric weight-based glucose load capped at 75 g. Screening precedes symptoms. Insulin is the established treatment; A1c alone and routine substitution of oral drugs do not follow this guidance.

choiceReview.text: Screen during stable health and monitor glucose more intensively during illness, glucocorticoids, pregnancy, or enteral feeding.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Use the same annual fasting-only test in every clinical situation.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Delay glucose assessment until all continuous feeding has been stopped.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Skip additional assessment during systemic glucocorticoids if A1c is normal.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Stable-health OGTT does not replace situational monitoring. Acute exacerbation treatment needs fasting and two-hour postprandial measurements, and continuous feeding needs mid- and immediate postfeeding measurements. Pregnancy has additional screening requirements.

choiceReview.text: Review age, OGTT, fasting and postprandial glucose, symptoms, A1c limits, weight, lung function, feeds, steroids, pregnancy, and insulin plan.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review A1c alone and omit the OGTT and feeding schedule.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review fasting glucose alone and omit postprandial readings during acute illness.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review the insulin prescription but omit nutritional and pulmonary goals.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Interpret glucose in its timing and clinical context, with nutritional and treatment information. A1c-only or fasting-only assessment can miss CF dysglycemia; insulin care must preserve appropriate nutrition.

choiceReview.text: A normal A1c can falsely reassure because CF dysglycemia may be postprandial and A1c can be deceptively low.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Using OGTT for annual screening during stable health
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Confirming elevated home-meter readings with laboratory plasma glucose
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Using A1c to help monitor established CFRD without treating it as the sole screening test
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: A normal A1c does not rule out CFRD. OGTT screening and confirmation of meter abnormalities are appropriate. A1c retains a monitoring role after diagnosis, which is distinct from relying on it alone to screen.

choiceReview.text: CF bone risk reflects nutrition, vitamin D, inflammation, low weight, inactivity, endocrine disease, glucocorticoids, transplant exposure, and age.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: CF bone loss is caused only by low vitamin D.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Good pulmonary symptoms eliminate bone risk from steroids or delayed puberty.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: A normal weight makes fracture history irrelevant.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: CF bone risk reflects multiple nutritional, endocrine, inflammatory, activity, and treatment factors. Vitamin D alone, respiratory symptoms alone, or one weight measurement cannot capture that risk.

choiceReview.text: Schedule bone-density and laboratory assessment by age and risk, correct reversible causes, and treat established disease when indicated.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Wait for a fracture before any adult DXA assessment.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Give vitamin D alone without reviewing fractures, bone density, or endocrine disease.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Begin identical bisphosphonate treatment for every patient regardless of bone density or risk.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: CF guidance uses age and risk for DXA and combines reversible-factor treatment with density and fracture assessment. Pharmacotherapy requires clinical indications and individual review, not universal treatment or waiting for injury.

choiceReview.text: Review fractures, height loss, nutrition, vitamin D, calcium, weight-bearing activity, puberty, hormones, glucocorticoids, transplant, kidney function, and DXA.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review vitamin D alone and omit prior fractures and DXA.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review DXA alone and omit glucocorticoids, puberty, and nutritional status.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review calcium intake alone and omit weight-bearing activity and transplant status.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Bone surveillance integrates fracture, density, nutrition, activity, endocrine and treatment risks. Each narrower alternative omits factors that can change management.

choiceReview.text: Replacing vitamin D without assessing the broader fracture phenotype can leave major drivers of bone loss untreated.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Reviewing glucocorticoid exposure alongside vitamin status
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Assessing delayed puberty, hypogonadism, and fracture history
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Using age and clinical risk to decide when DXA is needed
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Vitamin D replacement is one component of prevention and treatment. Steroids, endocrine factors, fracture history and density require assessment; the other choices describe appropriate broader care.

choiceReview.text: Liver and kidney surveillance must inform medication selection, dose, toxicity monitoring, and transplant planning throughout CF care.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Normal transaminases exclude clinically important portal disease.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: A normal creatinine excludes every renal concern regardless of low muscle mass.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Organ surveillance can be deferred while the drug regimen remains unchanged.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Structural liver disease and renal trajectory matter to medication safety. Liver enzymes or creatinine in isolation can miss clinically important context; surveillance should not depend only on a medication change.

choiceReview.text: Trend organ function and structural disease, then adjust nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, and renally or hepatically cleared treatment accordingly.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Continue the same high-risk drug doses despite a major change in kidney function.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Wait for jaundice before evaluating persistent liver-test abnormalities.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Interpret a low creatinine as proof of excellent filtration without considering malnutrition.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Organ function and structural disease must inform exposure and monitoring. Changing renal function, persistent liver abnormalities, and low muscle mass require evaluation rather than a fixed-dose or single-value assumption.

choiceReview.text: Review liver chemistry, platelets, imaging, portal signs, creatinine, filtration, hydration, stones, diabetes, aminoglycosides, modulators, and transplant medicines.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review AST and ALT alone and omit platelets, cholestatic tests, and imaging.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review one creatinine alone and omit prior results, hydration, and nephrotoxic drugs.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review modulator adherence alone and omit other medications and liver history.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Liver assessment includes bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, GGT, platelets, and imaging context. Renal safety requires trajectory and exposure review. Single-domain alternatives omit important evidence.

choiceReview.text: Waiting for jaundice or creatinine elevation alone can miss earlier portal disease or cumulative kidney injury.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Following platelets and liver/spleen imaging when clinically indicated
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Interpreting creatinine alongside nutritional status and renal trajectory
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Reviewing nephrotoxic exposures during antibiotic treatment
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Waiting for jaundice or creatinine elevation alone can delay recognition. Platelet/imaging assessment and renal trajectory or exposure review are appropriate safeguards.

choiceReview.text: Adults with CF need earlier colorectal cancer screening, with additional risk and modified timing after solid-organ transplantation.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: CF uses average-risk colorectal screening without transplant modifications.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Solid-organ transplantation lowers CF colorectal cancer risk.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Annual stool testing is an established equivalent to colonoscopy for CF screening.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: CF guidance recommends colonoscopy from age 40 and modified timing after transplant from age 30. Stool testing has insufficient evidence as an equivalent, and transplantation increases rather than reduces risk.

choiceReview.text: Apply current CF-specific screening age, interval, and bowel preparation while investigating alarm symptoms diagnostically.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Apply average-risk screening intervals regardless of CF or prior polyps.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Use routine bowel preparation without discussing the CF regimen.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Wait for the next screening date despite new bleeding or obstructive symptoms.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: CF-specific timing, preparation, and prior findings affect surveillance. New alarm symptoms need diagnostic evaluation; the routine schedule is not a reason to defer it.

choiceReview.text: Review age, transplant status, prior colonoscopy and preparation, polyps, family history, bleeding, anemia, bowel change, obstruction, and follow-up interval.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Review age alone and omit transplant history and the last colonoscopy.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review a prior colonoscopy date but omit preparation quality and polyp findings.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Review screening eligibility but omit bleeding, anemia, and bowel change.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Transplant, prior examination quality and pathology, and current symptoms determine the next evaluation. Age or dates alone cannot establish the correct plan.

choiceReview.text: Using average-risk screening timing can delay detection in a population with increased and earlier colorectal cancer risk.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Planning more intensive CF bowel preparation with the endoscopist
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Using prior adenomatous polyp findings to shorten surveillance
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Evaluating new alarm symptoms before a routine screening date
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Average-risk timing can delay CF screening. Intensive preparation, polyp-based surveillance, and prompt diagnostic evaluation are appropriate components of the CF plan.

choiceReview.text: 6,400 units/kg/day
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: 1,600 units/kg/day
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: 4,800 units/kg/day
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: 8,000 units/kg/day
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Eight capsules provide 192,000 units/day; dividing by 30 kg gives 6,400 units/kg/day. The 1,600 figure describes one meal, 4,800 omits the snacks, and 8,000 would require ten capsules.

choiceReview.text: Each meal is below 2,500 units/kg, but the daily total is 11,000 units/kg and requires investigation.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: The daily total is 6,000 units/kg because snacks do not count.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: The daily total is 7,000 units/kg because only one snack is counted.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Every boundary is satisfied because each meal is below 2,500 units/kg.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Three meals give 6,000 units/kg/day and five snacks give 5,000, totaling 11,000. This exceeds the daily investigation boundary even though each meal is below its separate limit.

choiceReview.text: Measure midway through and immediately after feeding at initiation, then at these times monthly at home; confirm elevated meter readings in the laboratory.
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Measure fasting glucose alone annually and ignore the feeding window.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Use A1c alone monthly without timed glucose readings.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Measure only before the feed and diagnose CFRD from any single elevated home-meter reading.
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: Continuous-feed screening targets mid- and immediate postfeeding glucose, initially and monthly thereafter. Fasting-only or A1c-only testing can miss feeding-related dysglycemia, and elevated meter values need laboratory confirmation.

choiceReview.text: At the diagnosis of advanced liver disease, then annually
choiceReview.assessment: best answer supported in stated context

choiceReview.text: Only at age 10 regardless of liver disease
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Only after a high A1c or diabetes symptoms appear
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

choiceReview.text: Only after solid-organ transplantation
choiceReview.assessment: incorrect or inappropriate in the stated question context; see the individually reviewed rationale

wholeQuestionReview.alternativeReasoning: The 2024 CF hepatobiliary guidance recommends screening from advanced-liver-disease diagnosis, even before age 10, then annually. Waiting for age 10, symptoms, A1c elevation, or transplantation misses that higher-risk recommendation.

sourceDiscrepancies.finding: Book meal-or-daily wording does not establish permission to ignore a separate limit;current Creon labeling and CFF guidance require applicable investigation checks. Fat-based daily limit absent from book;official supplement explicitly recorded.
Historic high-calorie counseling qualified using current phenotype and modulator response;no blanket calorie or salt restriction.
Website states24-48weeks;original guideline states24-28weeks. No adoption of website typo;this unit does not add numeric pregnancy schedules.
Displayed recommendation15 appears twice;second is painmanagement. Read all25recommendations;do not infer a missing clinical recommendation.
Original diagnostic feeding row says exceeds200mg/dL;summary saysatleast200mg/dL. This unit teaches screening and laboratory confirmation,not a new exact feeding diagnostic cutoff.
Book 8h minimum vs6h table/counseling retained for pending airway/antimicrobial unit;not resolved or published by nutrition unit.
Older page adult cartridge wording not treated as current device eligibility. No age,formula,flow-rate oruniversal tube protocol asserted.
Observational CFRD association does not prove causation;exacerbation proxy did not establish cumulative IV-aminoglycoside CKD effect. Acute nephrotoxicity preserved.
